strengths: The paper presents a clear and potentially useful formalization of recursive language models using a minimal call/return interface, with an intuitive distinction between active local context and global stack storage.

The theoretical contribution is ambitious and reasonably well connected to classical results on alternating computation, space complexity, and recursive machines. The stated hierarchy between no recursion, constant-depth recursion, and unbounded recursion provides an interesting perspective on agentic systems.
The manuscript is generally well organized and readable. Definitions, resource measures, pseudocode, and proof structure make the main ideas accessible despite the technical subject matter.

The SAT results are promising: the fine-tuned 3B recursive model reaches 98%, 95%, and 64% accuracy on the three difficulty levels, and the trajectory-versus-active-context plot qualitatively demonstrates the intended behavior.

The appendix reports several useful implementation details, including the base model, optimizer, learning rate, epochs, context length, hardware, data-generation algorithm, and examples of recursive traces.
The work has no evident direct ethical concern; its discussion of error propagation is useful, although the broader impact statement is brief.
weaknesses: The decisive empirical weakness is the absence of a matched non-recursive control. The proposed model is supervised on benchmark-specific DPLL traces, while the reported frontier models are prompted baselines imported from prior work. Consequently, Table 1 cannot establish that recursion, rather than task-specific fine-tuning or DPLL supervision, causes the improvement. A Qwen2.5-3B model trained on equivalent non-recursive traces, plus call/return and root-prefix ablations, is essential.

The evaluation is narrow and statistically weak: it uses only 100 examples per difficulty level, reports no confidence intervals or multiple training/inference seeds, and evaluates only one task whose standard solver already has exactly the recursive structure used for supervision. The claimed transfer beyond the training distribution is not established merely by moving from lower-clause to higher-clause instances.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper omits the number of training examples, sampling seeds, decoding settings, inference limits, failure handling, exact baseline prompts and budgets, numerical data underlying Figure 3, and any code or checkpoint availability statement.

Several conclusions overstate what the theory establishes in practice. The basic simulation in Theorem 1 requires double-exponentially many generated tokens; reducing this to the simulated time requires an added memoization and retrieval mechanism not present in the minimal recursive model. Thus the result primarily concerns expressivity under unconstrained global storage and time, not a demonstrated efficient long-horizon reasoning method.

The claimed GS/LS inference speedup is unsupported. Summarization-based systems do not necessarily attend to the entire historical trajectory after compression, and the analysis ignores cache transfer, stack management, recursive-call generation, and latency. No wall-clock, FLOP, memory, or token-cost comparison is reported.

There are formal gaps in the realizability arguments. Crucial Transformer primitives and canonicalization are largely delegated to prior work rather than constructed here. Moreover, the stated configuration embedding walks through the nonblank interval yet must end at the head position, which may lie outside that interval on a blank cell; as written, this does not encode every reachable Turing-machine configuration.

The computational model needs stronger uniformity assumptions. Positional embeddings are defined as an unrestricted map over all positions, while the upper-bound arguments implicitly require them and the numerical operations to be finitely describable and efficiently simulable. Without that condition, the claimed complexity characterizations are not fully justified.

The limitations discussion acknowledges error accumulation but does not adequately address the dominant limitations: unlimited external storage assumptions, potentially enormous computation, I/O overhead, benchmark-specific algorithm distillation, and the lack of evidence on less naturally decomposable tasks. Overall, the theoretical perspective is valuable, but the empirical evidence and several formal details need substantial revision before the central practical and optimality claims are reliable.

strengths: The paper presents a clean, minimal call/return abstraction for recursive language-model inference and clearly distinguishes local active-context space from total stack storage.

The theoretical component is ambitious and technically substantive. It connects recursive Transformers to classical time/space and alternating-machine results, provides explicit simulation constructions, and extends the analysis to a broad oracle-scaffold model of agentic systems.
The manuscript is generally well organized and readable, with useful pseudocode, formal definitions, and extensive proof appendices. The SAT example makes the proposed mechanism concrete.

The idea of synthesizing recursion, bounded-context Transformers, and agentic scaffolds into one complexity-theoretic framework offers useful conceptual understanding, even though recursion itself and several underlying complexity results are not new.

The SAT results are promising: the fine-tuned 3B model reaches 98%, 95%, and 64% accuracy across the three reported difficulty levels, and the trajectory/context measurements illustrate how recursive execution can keep individual contexts bounded.
The work raises no clear material ethical concern; SAT is a low-risk evaluation domain and the impact statement identifies the general dual-use nature of capability improvements.
weaknesses: The experiment does not isolate the contribution of recursion. A Qwen2.5-3B model supervised on DPLL traces is compared mainly against general-purpose models using results imported from another paper. There is no matched non-recursive Qwen fine-tuning baseline, shallow-recursion baseline, summarization baseline, or model trained on equivalent solver traces. The gains therefore could come from task-specific supervision rather than recursive execution.

The empirical evidence is too narrow for the broad practical claims. It covers one synthetic SAT benchmark with only 100 test instances per difficulty level, reports no confidence intervals or significance tests, and provides no results on other long-horizon tasks. The 64% versus 52.9% hard-set comparison may be noisy at this sample size.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The paper gives optimizer-level training details but omits the training-set size, random seeds, decoding parameters, inference budgets, stopping/failure rules, maximum recursion depth, prompt details for all baselines, and code or generated traces. It is also unclear whether the reported baseline evaluations used comparable prompts and compute.

The theoretical results are repeatedly interpreted more broadly than they establish. Theorems 1–5 are expressivity statements for idealized, constant-size exact-arithmetic Transformers and bounded deterministic scaffolds; they do not establish that learned LLMs can discover the decompositions, remain reliable at exponential depth, or obtain practical efficiency improvements.

The claim of an exponential context advantage hides severe resource costs. The main simulation may require exponential recursion depth and double-exponential generated tokens; reducing this to the original time bound requires memoizing and retrieving subproblems in an external memory mechanism that is not part of the basic recursive model.

Section 6.1's claimed GS/LS inference speedup is not justified. A summarization-based single-context system discards old context and need not attend over the full global trajectory, while recursive execution incurs stack storage, KV-cache transfer, and restoration costs. No wall-clock, FLOP, memory-transfer, or end-to-end cost measurement supports the stated speedup.

The claimed optimality over agentic systems is only complexity-class optimality under restrictive local-space and oracle-computability assumptions. It does not imply that richer orchestration cannot improve time, sample efficiency, reliability, parallelism, communication, or constants, so statements that orchestration offers 'no additional power' need substantial qualification.

Several Transformer realizability arguments delegate essential operations, including canonicalization and exact-match retrieval, to constructions in prior work instead of proving them fully here. This makes the central theory difficult to verify independently and leaves uniformity and implementation assumptions insufficiently exposed.

The limitations discussion is incomplete and sometimes dismissive. It does not seriously address the extreme runtime/storage costs, matched-baseline problem, dependence on oracle-generated DPLL traces, limited task coverage, or the difficulty of auditing erroneous returned subresults. Discarding a child's reasoning does not mitigate an incorrect returned answer and may make diagnosis harder.

Overall, the formal perspective has merit, but the current evidence does not support the paper's broad claims of practical superiority, efficiency, or learned long-horizon generalization. Matched ablations, broader evaluations, complete reproducibility details, and substantially narrower claims are needed before acceptance.

strengths: Soundness: The manuscript gives a coherent formal model of call/return recursion, distinguishes local from global space, and supports its main complexity results with substantial constructions and proofs, including two routes to the deep-recursion result. Significance: Formalizing recursion depth and active-context length as resources provides a useful perspective on long-horizon LLM and agentic computation. The connection between bounded local context, recursive scaffolding, and classical time/space classes could inform future system design.

Originality: Although recursive machines and related complexity results are classical, connecting them explicitly to Transformer-driven call/return systems and extending the analysis to general recursive agentic scaffolds offers a meaningful new synthesis.

Empirical results are promising: the fine-tuned 3B recursive model obtains 98%, 95%, and 64% accuracy on easy, medium, and hard SATBench instances, respectively, exceeding the reported much larger prompted models. Generalization to hard instances excluded from training is encouraging.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized. The formal definitions, algorithms, diagrams, implementation template, training hardware, optimizer settings, and representative traces make the proposed mechanism understandable.
weaknesses: Soundness of the empirical attribution is the main concern. The recursive model receives supervised fine-tuning on DPLL traces, whereas the frontier-model results are imported standard-prompting baselines. There is no equivalently fine-tuned non-recursive Qwen2.5-3B baseline, context-management baseline, or call/return ablation. Consequently, the experiment does not establish that recursion—rather than domain-specific algorithm distillation—causes the accuracy gain.

The evaluation is narrow and statistically weak: it uses one task family and only 100 examples per difficulty level, with no confidence intervals, multiple training seeds, or significance tests. SAT also supplies the recursive decomposition through a hand-engineered DPLL trace generator, so the evidence does not yet show that models learn decomposition on less structured tasks.

The context-efficiency evidence lacks a matched baseline and does not report accuracy as a function of context budget, recursion depth, runtime, latency, memory movement, or token cost. Active contexts in Figure 3 appear mostly within the 4096-token training window, making the claimed practical advantage over competitive context-management methods difficult to quantify.

Section 6.1 overstates the inference comparison. A summarization system does not necessarily attend to every token in its complete historical trajectory after old text is discarded; therefore, the asserted GS/LS speedup over any single-context model does not follow as written. Restoring suspended KV caches and external-memory traffic may also impose substantial unmeasured overhead.

The theoretical results concern idealized hard-attention Transformers with exact logarithmic-precision arithmetic. Several essential realizability operations, especially canonicalization and sequence processing, are delegated to prior work rather than constructed fully here. The manuscript should more carefully separate conclusions about this formal model from claims about practical finite-precision LLMs.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The number of training instances, exact train/validation split, random seeds, decoding parameters, stopping safeguards, baseline prompts, dataset identifiers, and code/model release information are missing. Left truncation may also affect recursive traces, but its frequency and impact are not reported.

The wording sometimes exceeds what is demonstrated, particularly claims that recursion is the exclusive source of additional agentic power, that any computable problem is practically modularizable, and that the physical attention limit is no longer a fundamental barrier. The formal constructions can require exponential recursion depth and double-exponential work without memoization, limiting their practical implication.

The limitations discussion acknowledges error propagation but omits the more decisive limitations: dependence on oracle-generated decompositions, absence of controlled baselines, narrow evaluation, extreme theoretical runtime, and external-storage costs. The ethics statement is generic; risks associated with scaling autonomous recursive agents deserve at least brief consideration.
